results.prompt: How do I monitor my deployed workflow's execution history and logs in Chainlink CRE?
results.answer:
I'll search for information about monitoring workflow execution in Chainlink CRE.# Monitoring Your Deployed Workflow in Chainlink CRE

After deploying a workflow in Chainlink CRE, you can track its execution history, performance metrics, and logs in two main ways: through the **CRE web UI** and through the **CRE CLI**.

## Using the CRE Web UI (primary method)

After deploying a workflow, you can monitor its execution history, performance metrics, and logs through the CRE web interface. To get started:

1. Log in to the CRE UI at app.chain.link/cre/discover.
2. Navigate to the Workflows section by clicking Workflows in the left sidebar, or visit app.chain.link/cre/workflows directly.

**The Workflows dashboard** gives you an org-wide view. The dashboard displays three main sections: Recent executions, which shows the most recent workflow runs across all your workflows; an Activity chart that visualizes successful and unsuccessful executions over the selected time period; and an All workflows table that lists all deployed workflows in your organization. You can use the dropdown menu to adjust the time range, and click on any workflow row to view its detailed performance and execution history.

**Drilling into a single workflow** — once you click a workflow, you get a dedicated monitoring page. When you click on a workflow, you'll see a dedicated page with comprehensive monitoring data, and the Performance chart shows execution trends for this specific workflow over the selected time period. This helps you identify patterns, track reliability, and spot anomalies.

**The Execution tab** — this is where the run history lives. The Overview panel displays key workflow metadata, and the Execution tab shows a detailed table of all workflow runs. To find problems quickly, use the ALL dropdown filter to view all executions, only successful ones, or only failures — this lets you quickly identify failures.

**Viewing detailed logs and events** — click on any execution ID to view detailed logs and events for that specific run. There are two important tabs here:
- The Events tab shows system-level events only.
- To see your custom log messages (e.g., runtime.log() in TypeScript or logger.Info() in Go), switch to the Logs tab, which shows only user-emitted logs from your workflow code.

When a run fails, for deployed workflows you'll see it in the Execution tab with a Failure status and the error message in the Logs tab.

## Using the CRE CLI

The CLI provides a command specifically for pulling logs from an execution: `cre execution logs` shows the log lines emitted during an execution. More broadly, CRE supports workflow lifecycle management to deploy, activate, pause, update, and delete workflows through the CLI, and monitoring and debugging to access detailed logs, events, and performance metrics in the CRE UI.

## Tracking a specific execution (e.g., HTTP-triggered runs)

If you trigger a workflow via an HTTP request, you can trace that exact run. Copy the workflow_execution_id to track this specific execution in the CRE UI — you can view logs, events, and execution details using this ID. Then, in the UI: go to app.chain.link/cre/workflows, click on your workflow, check the Execution tab for recent runs, and click on an Execution ID to view detailed logs and events.

---

**In short:** Use the **CRE UI Workflows dashboard → your workflow → Execution tab** to see run history and performance, then click an **Execution ID** and toggle between the **Events** (system-level) and **Logs** (your custom log output) tabs. For a command-line workflow, use `cre execution logs`. For the full walkthrough, see Chainlink's [Monitoring & Debugging Workflows](https://docs.chain.link/cre/guides/operations/monitoring-workflows) guide.

results.prompt: In Chainlink CRE, where do my custom logger.Info() messages from my Go workflow show up in the dashboard?
results.answer:
Your custom `logger.Info()` output shows up in the **CRE monitoring dashboard (the CRE web interface)**, tied to individual workflow executions.

Here's how it works:

- After deploying a workflow, you can monitor its execution history, performance metrics, and logs through the CRE web interface.

- To find your specific log lines, you drill into an execution from the dashboard. When you see red bars in the chart or failed executions, you click through to view logs and identify the root cause. The same click-through works for successful executions too — that's where the log output for each run lives.

- The Go `logger.Info()` call is exactly the mechanism the docs recommend for producing these messages (the equivalent of `runtime.log()` in the TypeScript SDK). The docs even encourage you to use descriptive log messages and include context in your log statements to make debugging easier, showing examples like `logger.Info("Successfully fetched offchain value", "result", offchainValue)` — and the key/value pairs you pass become part of the structured log entry.

**Practical tips:**
- On the dashboard, use the **Activity chart** to spot the execution you care about, then click into that execution to see its associated logs including your `logger.Info()` lines.
- If you want to see logs *before* deploying, you can run the workflow locally with the CRE CLI simulator, where log output prints to your terminal instead of the dashboard.

results.prompt: My Chainlink CRE workflow isn't executing at all — no recent executions show up in the dashboard. What should I check?
results.answer:
I'll search for current information on troubleshooting Chainlink CRE workflows that aren't executing.I ran into a search rate limit before I could pull in extensive documentation, so much of the checklist below draws on general Chainlink CRE architecture. I was able to confirm one relevant detail from the Chainlink docs, which I've cited. Here's a systematic way to diagnose a workflow that shows no executions:

## 1. Confirm the workflow is actually deployed and active
- Verify the workflow was successfully **deployed/registered** (not just compiled locally). A failed deployment often produces no runtime records at all.
- Check the workflow's **status** — if it's **paused** rather than active, it won't run. Resume it if needed.
- Make sure you're viewing the **correct workflow owner address, project, and environment** in the dashboard. A very common cause of "no executions" is simply looking at the wrong owner/project scope.

## 2. Investigate the trigger — this is the most likely culprit
"No executions at all" usually means the trigger never fired. The fix depends on your trigger type:

- **Cron / time-based trigger:** Double-check the schedule expression. An invalid or overly-long interval, or a misconfigured cron string, means it never fires.
- **HTTP trigger:** These are **pull-based** — nothing runs until an external request actually hits the gateway. Confirm you're sending the request correctly. If the request fails (e.g., invalid JWT, unauthorized key, workflow not found), the gateway returns an error response. So check for auth/JWT and key issues on the caller side.
- **EVM log / on-chain event trigger:** Verify the contract address, chain, and event signature/filter are correct, and that matching events are genuinely being emitted on-chain during your test window.

For HTTP triggers specifically, once a request succeeds, you can copy the workflow_execution_id to track that specific execution in the CRE UI, and view logs, events, and execution details using this ID. If you never get an execution ID back, the trigger request itself is being rejected before execution.

## 3. Check deployment configuration
- **DON assignment:** Confirm the workflow is targeting a valid DON that is actually running and able to pick it up.
- **Config / secrets:** Missing or malformed config or secrets can cause failures — though note this typically appears as *failed* executions rather than *no* executions.
- **Binary/compilation:** Ensure the compiled WASM binary uploaded correctly and matches what was registered.

## 4. Check identity and permissions
- Confirm the **owner key/address** used for deployment matches what you expect and is authorized.
- Verify the account/DON meets any **funding or registration requirements** for your environment.

## Suggested order of attack
1. Verify you're looking at the right owner/project/environment in the dashboard.
2. Confirm the workflow status is **active**, not paused, and that deployment succeeded.
3. Focus hard on the **trigger** — for HTTP, manually send a request and check for an error/execution ID; for cron, validate the schedule; for EVM, confirm events are emitting.
4. Only then dig into config/secrets/DON if you see executions *attempting* but failing.

If you can tell me **which trigger type** you're using (cron, HTTP, or on-chain event) and whether the deployment itself reported success, I can narrow this down considerably — and I can run more targeted searches against the CRE docs once the rate limit clears.

results.prompt: CRE workflows dashboard filter failed executions
results.answer:
Here's how to filter for failed workflow executions in the Chainlink CRE (Chainlink Runtime Environment) dashboard.

## Using the Web Dashboard

Navigate to the Workflows section by clicking Workflows in the left sidebar, or visit app.chain.link/cre/workflows directly (after logging in to the CRE UI at app.chain.link/cre/discover).

The Workflows dashboard is organized into a few areas: Recent executions shows the most recent workflow runs across all your workflows, the Activity chart visualizes successful and unsuccessful executions over the selected time period, and the All workflows table lists all deployed workflows with their status and execution history.

To isolate failures: To quickly identify failures, use the filter dropdown to show only failed executions. This helps you focus on debugging problematic runs.

Once filtered, you can drill into a specific run: the top section displays the most recent workflow executions across your organization, each showing an Execution ID, workflow name, a Success or Failure status indicator, and a timestamp — and you can click on any execution ID to view detailed logs and events for that specific run.

For a single failed run, you'll see it in the Execution tab with a Failure status and the error message in the Logs tab.

## Using the CLI

If you prefer the command line, the CRE CLI supports the same filtering:

- cre execution list — List recent executions; filter by workflow, status, and time range
- cre execution status — Show detailed status for a single execution; cre execution events — Show the capability event timeline for an execution; and cre execution logs — Show log lines emitted during an execution.

So to see only failed runs, use `cre execution list` with a status filter, then use `cre execution logs` (or the execution ID's Logs tab in the UI) to see the underlying error.

---

Here's how logging generally works in CRE workflows so your messages surface in the **Logs tab** of the CRE UI / CLI simulation output.

## Key concept

In CRE, you don't use the language's raw `console.log`/`fmt.Println` for observable logs. Instead you use the **logger provided by the workflow `Runtime`** that's passed into your handler/callback. Logs emitted through that runtime logger are captured by the CRE platform and rendered in the **Logs tab**.

## TypeScript

The runtime object passed to your handler exposes a logger. A typical pattern:

```typescript
import { cre, type Runtime } from "@chainlink/cre-sdk"

// The handler receives the runtime (and trigger payload)
const onCronTrigger = (runtime: Runtime<Config>): string => {
  // Descriptive log statements — these appear in the Logs tab
  runtime.log("Workflow execution started")

  const now = new Date().toISOString()
  runtime.log(`Handling cron trigger at ${now}`)

  try {
    const result = doWork(runtime)
    runtime.log(`Work completed successfully: result=${result}`)
    return result
  } catch (err) {
    runtime.log(`Work failed: ${String(err)}`)
    throw err
  }
}
```

Notes:
- The logger method is commonly `runtime.log(...)`. In some SDK versions it's exposed as `runtime.logger` or a `Logger()` accessor — check the "SDK Reference: Core" page.
- Pass a single string. Interpolate values with template literals since structured fields may not render.
- Because a workflow can run across multiple nodes in a DON, keep messages descriptive enough to trace which step produced them.

## Go

In Go, the runtime exposes a logger — typically a standard library `*slog.Logger` via `runtime.Logger()`:

```go
func onCronTrigger(config *Config, runtime cre.Runtime, trigger *cron.Payload) (string, error) {
    logger := runtime.Logger()

    // Descriptive log statements — these appear in the Logs tab
    logger.Info("Workflow execution started")

    logger.Info("Handling cron trigger",
        "scheduledTime", trigger.ScheduledExecutionTime.AsTime(),
    )

    result, err := doWork(runtime)
    if err != nil {
        logger.Error("Work failed", "error", err)
        return "", err
    }

    logger.Info("Work completed successfully", "result", result)
    return result, nil
}
```

Notes:
- Because it's `slog`-style, you pass a message string followed by **key/value pairs** for structured context (`"key", value`), which is the idiomatic Go approach and renders as structured attributes.
- Use `logger.Info`, `logger.Warn`, `logger.Error`, `logger.Debug` for severity levels — the level is shown in the Logs tab and lets you filter.

## Viewing the logs

- **Local simulation:** run your workflow with the CRE CLI (e.g. `cre workflow simulate ...`); logs print to your terminal.
- **Deployed workflow:** open the workflow in the CRE UI and select the **Logs tab** for a given execution to see the emitted messages, timestamps, and severity.

## Practical tips
- Log at boundaries: start of handler, before/after external calls (HTTP, EVM reads/writes), and on error paths.
- Include identifiers (trigger time, request ID, target address) so you can correlate entries.
- Avoid logging secrets or full sensitive payloads.
- Prefer levels (`Info`/`Warn`/`Error`) so you can filter noise in production.

---

## Viewing Credit Consumption and Total Spend for CRE Workflows

You can find this information in the **CRE web interface (UI)**, not the CLI. After deploying a workflow, you can monitor its execution history, performance metrics, and logs through the CRE web interface.

**How to get there:**

1. Log in to the CRE UI at app.chain.link/cre/discover
2. Navigate to the Workflows section by clicking Workflows in the left sidebar, or visit app.chain.link/cre/workflows directly

**What you'll see:**

The Workflows dashboard displays three main sections: Recent executions, which shows the most recent workflow runs across all your workflows; an Activity chart, which visualizes successful and unsuccessful executions over the selected time period; and an All workflows table, which lists all deployed workflows with their status and execution history.

**For credits and total spend specifically:**

To track your overall cost, the documentation recommends that you track credit usage by monitoring the Total Workflow Spend to understand your workflow's cost over time.

So drilling into a specific deployed workflow in the Workflows dashboard lets you review its execution history (per-run activity) alongside the **Total Workflow Spend** metric, which aggregates the credits consumed across runs. You can also click through to view logs and identify the root cause for individual executions when you need to dig into what a particular run did.
